Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object

Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Here every submission is a program instead of a grid. To submit, write a Python function transform(grid) that

after 3 failed checks in an instance, a program's output is submitted without a check.

I'm not yet sure what transformation this task requires — the grid has scattered colored fragments (1s, 9s, 6s, 3s, 5s, 7s, 4s) on an 8 background, plus some 0s, and I can't confidently infer the rule from a single input. Getting a demonstration pair is cheap relative to a wrong guess.

{"action": "request_demos"}

The demo suggests: a special "reference" shape (color 2, an L-shape) and non-background shapes that are the same shape (up to scale/mirror) get recolored to the reference color. But in the test the reference appears to be the 0-shape (a domino), and it's unclear whether "matching shapes" means same topology at any scale (all straight lines?), same exact size, or a scaled-down copy. That's a big difference for the output. One more demo is worth it.

{"action": "request_demos"}

The demos show a "template" component (a unique-colored L-shape) and exactly one other component being recolored to the template's color — but I can't yet pin down *which* component qualifies (in demo 2, three identical single-cell components existed and only one was recolored, so position/alignment matters, not just shape). A wrong submission costs as much as a demo, so I'll gather more evidence.

{"action": "request_demos"}

I still can't pin down the selection rule. In demo 1 a small corner triomino was recolored to the template color; in demo 3 a 6-cell blob (congruent to a border-touching twin) was recolored; in demo 2 only a lone single cell changed. No single rule (shape match, congruent pair, size, alignment) explains all three, and guessing costs as much as another demo.

{"action": "request_demos"}

My rule passed all 4 demos but failed on the test, so my inference about the template/target selection must be off (possibly the template isn't the L-shape, or the target criterion differs). Rather than guess among several plausible alternatives (target = nearest object to template regardless of side; template = largest unique-color object; etc.), another demo is the cheaper way to disambiguate.

{"action": "request_demos"}
